extracted.intended_audience: Congressional policymakers, congressional staff, and DOD acquisition/oversight officials concerned with OMB Circular A-76 public-private competitions (especially at military medical facilities)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for conducting, overseeing, and legislating public-private (A-76) competitions — with special attention to the Walter Reed Army Medical Center case and implications for future military medical facility competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inherently governmental activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inherently governmental activity is an activity that is so intimately related to the public interest as to mandate performance by government personnel. It involves (1) binding the United States to take or not take action by contract, policy, regulation, authorization, order, or otherwise; (2) determining, protecting, and advancing economic, political, territorial, property, or other interests by military or diplomatic action, civil or criminal judicial proceedings, contract management, or otherwise; (3) significantly affecting the life, liberty, or property of private persons; or (4) exerting ultimate control over the acquisition, use, or disposition of United States property, including establishing policies or procedures for the collection, control, or disbursement of appropriated and other federal funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-part test from OMB Circular A-76 to classify activities as inherently governmental (and therefore not subject to competition). The Circular describes what makes activities inherently governmental; classification ultimately depends on several factors and is central to deciding whether a function is subject to A-76.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual inventory requirement (FAIR Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required under the Federal Activities Inventory Reform (FAIR) Act to prepare and submit annual inventories of commercial activities performed by Federal employees to OMB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain up-to-date inventories to identify which activities are commercial (potentially subject to competition) versus inherently governmental. This inventory is a prerequisite to applying A-76 to particular functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) as competition basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a business case analysis determines the work should be subject to competition, a Performance Work Statement (PWS) team develops a statement of the work to be performed. The statement is used as the basis for the competition. An agency must ensure that both the government's bid proposal and the private sector contractor's proposal reflect all of the functions and personnel called for in the PWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the PWS is comprehensive, stable, and consistently applied across government and contractor proposals; inaccuracies or repeated amendments to the PWS (the Walter Reed case cited ~1,500 changes) can undermine fairness and delay competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Most Efficient Organization (MEO) is developed by a team made up of federal employees and a private sector contractor; it is comprised of a group of federal employees and management's bid to perform the work as a streamlined reorganization (fewer people doing the work). The MEO is the basis for all Government costs entered on the cost-comparison form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO should realistically reflect how federal personnel would be organized to perform the work; it is developed from the Management Plan and PWS. The MEO exists only if it wins the competition; if it wins, a letter of obligation implements the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firewall between PWS team and MEO members
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules call for a 'firewall' that would prohibit all communication between members of the MEO and members serving on the PWS team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce strict separation to preserve fairness in the competition; communications that cross this firewall can create conflicts of interest and taint the competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum cost differential requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A-76 policy establishes a minimum cost differential, meaning no activities can be converted to or from performance by in-house federal employees to the private sector unless there is a minimal cost differential of $10 million or 10%. The MEO is required to show savings of at least $10 million or 10% over the private sector contractor's costs to win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the $10M/10% threshold to avoid conversions for 'marginal estimated savings.' This is a quantitative gate in the cost-comparison process and should be documented explicitly in cost analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines for A-76 studies (revised Circular)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Circular established new deadlines for completion of A-76 studies: 12 months for standard competitions, and 90 days for streamlined competitions. (Under earlier rules DOD was limited by law to a 30-month time frame.) Proposed legislation also considered limiting competitions to 540 days (~18 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to timeframes to reduce prolonged disruptions and attrition; extended multi-year competitions (Walter Reed took over six years) risk workforce destabilization and operational gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of competitive sourcing officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Circular required agencies to appoint competitive sourcing officials such as the Human Resource Advisor (HRA), Agency Tender Official (ATO), PWS Team Leader, Source Selection Authority (SSA), Contracting Officer (CO), and Competitive Sourcing Official (CSO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly designate roles and authorities up front; define responsibilities to ensure accountability and consistent application of procedures during all competition phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: PMA scorecard and competitive-sourcing goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive sourcing was a Presidential Management Agenda initiative, and OMB implemented a PMA scorecard (red-yellow-green) to evaluate agency progress; agencies (e.g., the Army) had numerical study goals to be achieved by set fiscal years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that externally-imposed numeric goals and scorecard incentives can create pressure to pursue studies even where inappropriate; oversight should account for goal-driven bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOD opt-out authority during war/mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: During times of declared war or military mobilization, the Department of Defense can opt out of the A-76 process. The DOD Competitive Sourcing Official shall determine if the circular applies to DOD in such times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use opt-out where mission demands make competitions counterproductive (Walter Reed testimony suggested not exercising this option led to personnel shortages during peak casualty loads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare retirement and health benefit costs (Section 322)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 322 requires that retirement costs be compared and that any potential retirement and health insurance benefits offered by potential contractors be comparable to current benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full life-cycle compensation (retirement, health benefits) in cost comparisons or explicitly document adjustments; failure to account for these can skew comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic requirement for competition at performance-period end (Section 323)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 323 amends 10 U.S.C. 2461 by not requiring DOD to automatically conduct a public-private competition under OMB Circular A-76, or any other provision of law, at the end of a performance period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow consideration of circumstances rather than an automatic trigger — provides flexibility to retain contractor performance when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insourcing preference and guidance (Section 324)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 324 provides for insourcing of certain new and contracted-out functions; it requires guidelines and procedures to ensure federal employees are considered to perform work currently performed by contractors and grants special consideration to activities associated with inherently governmental functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting legislative/regulatory guidance, require agencies to evaluate insourcing options and prioritize federal performance where justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit OPM influence over DOD competitions (Section 325)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 325 limits the influence of the Office of Personnel Management over DOD's conduct of public-private competitions or direct conversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify interagency roles and limit extraneous influence that might impede timely DOD decisionmaking; specify boundaries in statute/regulation to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded bid protest and 'interested party' rights (Section 326)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 326 amends the definition of who is an 'interested party' and grants bid protest rights to employee representatives designated as agent for the majority of affected employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure procedural rights for employee representatives to raise protests; define standing and timelines to allow effective challenge while preserving procurement timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller General expedited protest authority (Section 3557)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3557 grants certain authority to the Comptroller General to expedite actions in protests of public-private competitions under Circular A-76 and grants other rights to interested parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms for rapid resolution of protests to limit prolonged uncertainty; use expedited processes where appropriate to protect operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory competition threshold for 10+ civilian positions (Section 327)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 327 requires that a public-private competition be conducted (for executive agency functions performed by 10 or more agency civilian employees) before any activities may be converted to contractor performance, with certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numeric thresholds to trigger required procedures but accompany with substantive conditions and exemptions (e.g., mission-critical services, medical facilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition or limits on announcing/conducting competitions at military medical facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative provisions (e.g., Section 1676 in discussion) prohibit the announcement or conduct of A-76 competitions at military medical facilities unless certain conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat military medical facilities as a special category with higher thresholds or prohibitions for outsourcing given patient-care and readiness implications; require explicit conditions before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific reporting on status of ongoing A-76 competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could require specific reporting on the status of ongoing A-76 competitions to improve oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate regular, detailed reports (timelines, staffing impacts, cost-comparison data, implementation plans) to congressional defense committees to allow timely intervention where issues arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit establishment of numerical quotas for A-76 studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit the establishment of numerical quotas for A-76 studies to avoid pressure-driven competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid top-down numeric mandates that incentivize inappropriate or rushed competitions; focus oversight on quality and mission appropriateness rather than counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare activities at military medical facilities inherently governmental
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could declare all activities at military medical facilities to be inherently governmental, thereby exempting them from A-76 competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an option to protect continuity of care and staffing stability at sensitive medical facilities; consider narrow tailoring or exceptions rather than blanket rules if operationally necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit inclusion of health care and retirement costs in cost comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit the inclusion of health care and retirement costs from the A-76 cost-comparison process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding these costs would materially affect comparative outcomes; weigh equity for federal employees versus accurate reflection of total contractor costs in decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rotating team of acquisition professionals as Agency Tender Officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could establish a team of acquisition professionals to rotate service as Agency Tender Officials (ATOs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create institutional expertise and reduce single-person dependencies by rotating trained acquisition professionals into ATO roles; improves consistency and reduces capture/biased decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require enforcement of A-76 rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could require enforcement of the A-76 rules to ensure consistent and lawful conduct of competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate compliance audits, timelines, and penalties for procedural violations; independent oversight (GAO, IG) should be empowered to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal employees equivalent procedural rights as private contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could grant federal employees the same rights as private sector contractors (e.g., protest rights, representation) in the A-76 process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level the procedural playing field by ensuring employees and their representatives can meaningfully challenge process defects; define standing and remediation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage alternatives to A-76 (High-Performing Organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could encourage and incentivize alternatives to A-76 such as creating high-performing organizations (HPOs) to achieve efficiencies without competitive sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote HPO formation, metrics, and pilot programs as less disruptive ways to pursue efficiency; GAO CAP recommended HPOs as an alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancel outstanding A-76 studies conducted under pre-2003 Circular
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid problems similar to Walter Reed, Congress could direct cancellation of outstanding competitions conducted under the pre-2003 Circular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider retroactive cancellation where procedural regimes changed substantially and studies are stale or have caused prolonged instability (several multi-year competitions cited as problematic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for operational context and convergence-of-events risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether exogenous factors (e.g., wartime casualty surges, BRAC realignment, facility conditions, constrained resources) make A-76 competitions inappropriate or risk-prone in a given context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mission impact, staffing attrition risk, facility readiness, and concurrent policy actions before proceeding; the Walter Reed case showed how multiple converging factors can cause failure even if the process is followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure timely implementation after award to avoid service gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid long gaps between award decisions and contractor performance start-dates (Walter Reed: contractor awarded but did not begin until months later, producing staff shortages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include implementation timelines, transition plans, and holdback provisions in awards to prevent operational lapses during workforce transfers or hiring freezes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain leadership attention and avoid distraction by long-term restructuring (BRAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that BRAC/realignment decisions and long-term transition plans can place installations in 'limbo' that impedes capital improvements, recruitment, accreditation, and day-to-day leadership focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When overlapping major organizational changes with competitive sourcing, require mitigation plans (funding for interim maintenance, retention incentives, accelerated construction where needed) to preserve services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use independent review and audit throughout competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent reviews (e.g., GAO, Army Audit Agency, Independent Review Groups) are critical for oversight; the MEO's bid proposal was independently reviewed/certified by AAA in the Walter Reed case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize independent certification of cost estimates, PWS stability, and fairness of the process at key milestones to detect and correct errors early.
